While thematic similarities resonate through the collected works of all visionary artists, even the most self-aware amongst them might be hesitant to proclaim as a trilogy three decisively unique film projects unrelated in time and place and without a single character in common. Not so Terry Gilliam. For him, Time Bandits, Brazil and The Adventures of Baron Munchausen represent a three-part celebration of the persistent dreamer seeking refuge in flights of fancy from the humdrum realities of the workaday world. With massive doses of imagination - and an irreverent sense of humor springing from his Monty Python roots - Gilliam has spent the last decade leaping through time and space and into alternate universes both wondrous and bizarre. Acutely aware that special effects are the essential elements needed to unlock his wildest imaginings, Gilliam has surrounded himself with top practitioners in the field - some spanning all three pictures - who have consistently pushed the limits of budget-conscious, low-tech film trickery to produce for him an abundance of cinematic wonders both grand and small. In Time Bandits, he transported a young schoolboy across time and space in an adventure that spanned ten centuries and several continents. In Brazil, he plunged a middle-aged dreamer into the bureaucratic maw of a dystopic parallel universe. And now in The Adventures of Baron Munchausen, he has followed a mendacious old warrior through the skies and seas - even through the center of the earth and to the moon - in a captivating succession of very tall tales. In a decade of visionary work, Gilliam has explored the dark and light corners of his own boundless imagination and produced in the process a remarkable cinematic trilogy whose component elements somehow wound up with nothing at all in common - at least in the customary sense of shared characters or settings or even time frame. "Around the time Baron Munchausen was starting up," Gilliam recollected, "I began circulating the story that I was working on the fourth part of a trilogy. Initially I meant it as a joke. But somewhere along the line, I came to realize that there really was a trilogy. All three of my past films fall into a clear progression of sorts. Time Bandits concerns a youthful imagination trying to come to grips with the so-called 'real' world. Brazil concerns an adult imagination actively fleeing that real world - fleeing right into madness. And Munchausen concerns an old man's imagination battling the Age of Reason. In that instance - with the support of a young girl - imagination finally wins out over reality." Whatever its aesthetic connections, the Gilliam trilogy has clearly found its audience. Time Bandits - after being rejected by every major distributor in the business - at last found refuge with a small independent outlet and became an unexpected boxoffice smash. Its success helped spawn Brazil, which became an international cause celebre when its bleak vision of a 1984ish world caused Gilliam to lock horns with a major Hollywood studio -and win. The Adventures of Baron Munchausen proved controversial long before it was finished. While Gilliam battled to maintain control over his epic fantasy, the popular press circled like vultures as behind-the-scenes crises sent the budget skyrocketing out of control. For all the ulcers his films have generated, Gilliam and his vision have remained remarkably consistent and intact. Although he first gained prominence with the decidedly British 'Monty Python' comedy troupe in the early 1970s, Gilliam is in fact an American citizen, born in Minneapolis in 1940. When he was eleven, his family moved to Los Angeles where he subsequently attended high school and graduated from Occidental College. It was not his degree in political science, however - but rate his editonig but rather his editorship of the college humor magazine - that led Gilliam to New York and a place on the staff of Help!, a short-lived spin-off of Mad magazine. "Help! was basically a two-man operation, with Harvey Kurtzman doing the editing and me doing everything else. But it was an invaluable training ground really. Some of the best-known underground cartoonists - guys like Robert Crumb and Gilbert Shelton - got their start at Help/ I was also to meet a variety of interesting people there who would come in handy later on - people like John Cleese, for instance. It was during that period that I started making films. I saved up enough money to buy a spring-wound 16mm Bolex, and before long I was making all these silly little pixilated, flip-book types of films - people walking around doing foolish things." After Help! folded, Gilliam toured Europe for six months. "I really liked London above all else, but for some unfathomable reason I went back to L.A. and tried another career for a while - as the world's most uninvolved ad agency employee. Eventually I moved back to London - permanently, as it turned out - where I spent some time doing magazine work and illustration. By then, John Cleese was already well established in television and he introduced me to a couple of TV producers. Ultimately that led to my working on a little series called We Have Ways to Make You Laugh where I used to go on and draw caricatures of the guests. At one point they had some material that they wanted to present and I suggested animating it. They said okay - so suddenly I was an animator." Other television work followed - including a program titled Do Not Adjust Your Set, where Gilliam first met other soon-tobe Python members Eric Idle and Terry Jones. He even accomplished some feature film animation for the title sequence in Cry of the Banshee. But it was the late-night, low-budget comedy series Monty Python's Flying Circus that would catapult Gilliam to international renown. Concerning itself with educated, surreal comedy - as likely to mention Descartes as Daffy Duck - Python also featured weekly snippets of outrageous animation devised and executed by Gilliam. "I never had the will or the resources to do full animation for the Monty Python show. It was just too time consuming. I had to produce about two or three minutes of animation every two weeks and I was essentially doing it on my own with only one assistant. I was writing the material, drawing it when necessary, cutting it out, shooting it and doing all the sound effects. Obviously, anything more sophisticated would have been impossible. The Monty Python animation was shot on an Oxberry animation stand utilizing an old Mitchell camera that had been slightly modified for frame-by-frame work. I used to work with a fairly big field size that measured out at about thirty inches. Since the Python animation hinged on materials that were really just pieces of paper layered into five or six levels of art, it was necessary to work on a large field area. The large field also helped minimize some problems like excessive shadowing." Together with Terry Jones, Gilliam went on to codirect the first Python motion picture Monty Python and the Holy Grail. "Terry Jones and I had decided we wanted to be film directors, so we got the other Python members to agree that anybody named Terry would direct the first Python feature." Other solo efforts soon followed, including Jabberwocky and segments of Monty Python's The Meaning of Life and Monty Python's Life of Brian. By 1980, Gilliam had decided to break away from his support

group and direct a non-Python film titled Time Bandits. Even at this point, a recognizable and consistent artistic vision had begun to appear in his work. Gilliam's films were an odd mixture of stinging satire and low-brow humor laced with references to art and literature and a passion for recreating bygone cultures in a believable and realistic manner. "It's true that I have a deep love of history, literature and art. If I wanted to be shallow, I suppose I could just say that these are the results of a classic liberal arts education which involved philosophy, literature, o than have a social politics - the works. I would also like to think I have a social conscience, for whatever that's worth. But there is another level to my interests. I love to futz around with cartooning, I was always absorbed by the idea of ancient civilizations, as well as the art of such people as Goya and Brueghel, Dore and Piranesi. Hike movies, too - films by Disney and directors like Keaton and Kubrick and Fellini and Kurosawa - you know, the same ones Woody Allen likes. Further, I love to read. Dostoevsky is a favorite of mine - also Kurt Vonnegut and others. My favorite book is Catch-22. And this is why I made the boy in Time Bandits a reader. It was my little pitch to the children in the audience. 'Hey kids! See how this boy's parents only watch television? They get themselves blown up in the end! Save yourselves! Read!'' The central theme of Time Bandits, however - one which unites the film with both Brazil and Baron Munchausen - was a concept very close to the heart of its creator. "The one theme that runs through all three of these pictures is a consistently serious battle between fantasy and what people perceive as reality. What I dislike about so-called realists is that they seem to have a very limited view of the possibilities of the world. This rigid, authoritarian world-view we are putting up with right now limits the possibilities of other existent, just-as-credible parts of life. One of these 'parts' is the human imagination - which is, of course, what Munchausen, Brazil and Time Bandits are really all about." Imagination infuses Time Bandits. Costing just over $5 million to produce, Time Bandits was filmed during a twelve-week period in 1980 and released the following year. The film opens with a 'cosmic zoom-in' - a series of dissolves starting with a universal overview of stars and nebulae and ending at the home of Kevin (Craig Warnock), the young protagonist and lead character. "Obviously I was attempting to set up the vastness of the universe and then say, 'But here's this one small story," Gilliam explained. "But in terms of my trilogy, what's interesting about that sequence is that it introduces - in a rather spectacular way - my career-long association with Kent Houston of Peerless Camera Company Ltd. Peerless and Kent have handled the optical effects on all three of my past films." Peerless Camera is actually co-owned by Kent Houston and Terry Gilliam. "The company was formed in 1976," Gilliam recalled, "just after Holy Grail. I started buying up old Oxberrys and other things so I could set up my own effects unit." Houston CINEFEX 38 • 7

had actually begun working with Gilliam during the director's earliest television days. "Before that," Houston noted, "I had been with an English animator named Bob Godfrey, who made a minor splash in American television in the late 1960s with a short film called 'The Do-It-Yourself Cartoon Kit.' I was a rostrum cameraman for Bob, shooting a lot of flatbed animation. That's how I met Terry." Houston and Peerless were personally approached by Gilliam to handle the Time Bandits optical work. "Originally," said Houston, "the plan was to do as much of the effects work on stage as possible. But a lot of it just did not work out. So we became the salvage unit, doing a lot of cut and paste." Salvage work began with the very first sequence. "Essentially, the cosmic zoom was done with a combination of animation, crude computer controlled photography, NASA slides and a retouched aerial photograph. For the start of that shot, Terry had produced some artwork of arcane symbols. We shot that art as a series of acetate overlays on one of the first prototype digital computers in London. A company named Neilsen Hordell supplied the rig to us, which had been made by a guy named Mark Roberts. It was a real caveman number - the memory was in core rather than discs or tape. Very primitive. Basically, it was a computerized camera tied into an English version of an Oxberry stand. And we shot a lot of our Time Bandits animated material on that beast. In England, we tend - much more than in the United States - to use an underneath aerial image system on our animation stands. Essentially that's an animation stand which is used like a printer. A projector on the floor directs an image off a mirror underneath the stand up through a pair of large condensers set into the tabletop. Those condensers form an aerial image generated from the projector right onto the film - in-camera. If you put artwork such as mattes or titling on the tabletop - we did the Time Bandits titling ourselves - that artwork will be imaged into the camera as well. You can do quite good matting with this procedure. It also works well for combining animation with live-action. In general, we try to do as much in-camera compositing as we can, especially on anything that goes anywhere near an animation stand. We did have one other piece of equipment which became an effects workhorse on Time Bandits. This was our one and only optical printer that we owned at the time. It was a weird hybrid aerial image printer that was made in the early 1950s by a company called Eastern Effects in New York. We modified the drive and optics a bit, but basically this printer and the animation stand were the only bits of equipment we had to work with on Time Bandits." Included in the Time Bandits opticals crew were Tim Ollive and Paul Whitbread on the animation stand - assisted by Dennis De Groot - and Nick Dunlop on the optical printer. Terry Gilliam himself worked on the postproduction effects, including the starfield which is seen as a background element during the opening cosmic zoom. To make his starfield, Gilliam simply spattered white paint from a brush onto Astrolux - a shiny 8 - CINEFEX 38

black paper often used for this type of work. The director then enhanced the artwork with airbrushed nebulae and other graphic effects. "By adding in two or three different layers of stars and nebulae," Gilliam remarked, "you create a distinct parallax shift as you move through them. Real stars would never do that, of course, but by using this layered technique you get a great feeling of depth." After zooming in on a NASA-supplied slide of the earth, the image dissolves to an aerial view of Kevin's neighborhood - an endless sprawl of depressingly similar tract houses. "That was an actual aerial photograph that we extended a bit," Gilliam continued. "We'd gone to a London photo library and found this shot of a little town with rows and rows of identical tract homes. We reshot the photo, blew it up, painted out some of the homes on the edges and extended the image by painting in fields and such. Then we composited that with a very simple smoke overlay to give the illusion of clouds as we pushed in on it." Once inside young Kevin's home, we find his existence to be a lonely one. Ignored by his television-obsessed parents, unable to interest them in his enthusiasm for legendary heroes and ancient civilizations, Kevin retreats to his bedroom for a solitary night of reading. Then everything changes. "I decided we needed a really striking image to kick off Kevin's adventures," Gilliam recalled. "What could be more striking than a medieval knight crashing out of a bedroom wardrobe? We did that effect live - in-camera - at Lee International Studios in London, where we shot all the Time Bandits interiors. It was quite simply done. On a raised platform we built a false bedroom wall and an outsize version of the wardrobe itself which we made from balsa wood. Then we led the horse and rider up behind it, and the horse jumped through an opening in the back. That was the hard part. Just try to get a horse to leap into total blackness! Thankfully, he was a well-trained animal." The same physical setup was used for a later scene in which Kevin watches in astonishment as a gaggle of little people - the film's title characters - step out of his wardrobe. "I had an old circus gag in the back of my head for that," said Gilliam. "I always loved those little cars that would stop in a circus ring and expel a limitless number of clowns. And I loved the idea of working with a whole gang of little people throughout this particular picture. There were a couple of reasons - one was practical, one was not. My silly side was just tickled with the visual outrageousness of it all - with how I would be able to contrast the Bandits' heights with other objects in the film. From the very beginning, one of my ideas for Time Bandits had been to shoot the entire film from the eye level of a child. However, I then had serious reservations as to whether a kid could carry a whole movie. So I and my cowriter - Michael Palin - came up with the idea of using a gang of really short people who were the same size as the boy. Being able to get away with my original idea was the primary reason we ended up using little people on Time Bandits." The decision was not without its technical problems. "A lot of the film is shot with the camera about three feet off the ground or down in a hole - which is very hard on an operator's back. Nevertheless, I had no regrets. Until Time Bandits, no one had ever given little people a chance to be normal heroes in a film. So my actors all really threw themselves into their roles. They tried to do the most incredible things. In fact, I had to be careful to keep them from trying too hard and hurting themselves." Kevin's sense of confusion at finding his bedroom crowded with little people is soon replaced by fear - for the Bandits, he quickly discovers, are aptly dubbed. From their employer they have stolen a 'time hole map' - a rolled parchment pinpointing all the various rips in the fabric of time and space. Using this map as their guide, the pint-size renegades now intend to unabashedly pop in and out of various epochs simply to loot the riches of centuries gone by. Unfortunately for the Bandits, their employer - whom they identify as the Supreme Being - suddenly manifests himself in the form of a large disembodied head pronouncing dire threats of retribution. Terrified but unrepentant, the Bandits attempt to escape. Convinced that one of the bedroom walls is a portal to the past, they crowd against it and push - and to the astonishment of young Kevin, the wall yields to the pressure and begins to extend telescopically into a long white corridor. "The expanding corridor was actually quite simple," Gilliam recalled. "That was just a wooden tunnel about thirty-five feet long built at Lee International Studios. We dressed it with endless rolls of wallpaper. The moving wall itself was only a painted flat, snugly plugged into the corridor - it had wheels on its other side. All the actors had to do was push on this flat and it would slide right down the corridor. When we shot it, we pumped a lot of smoke and light into the set to suggest that the Supreme Being was coming after them." The floating head was not so simply achieved. "Originally we had built an elaborate rig that an actual actor would hang on - but we could not make it work. At the last minute I said: 'Scrap this. Cut me a head shape out of plywood about five feet tall. Paint it black. Just make it the silhouette of a head.' We did, and then hung this wooden shape off a long boom arm sticking out from a camera dolly. Then we pushed it down the corridor with smoke belching out behind and around it." "Months later," Houston continued, "Terry photographed a man named Edwin Finn - who had this wonderful skull-shaped head - reading the Supreme Being's lines against a wall on which Terry had drawn registration marks. Terry shot this on high-contrast black-and-white stock in order to wipe out the extraneous details on the man's face and give him a very simple, stylized look. We then took the Eastman color background plate of the plywood head and bipacked that with Terry's footage, taking the black-and-white material and shooting it as a separate exposure on the animation stand. We did this by making still enlargements of each frame and rephotographing them one at a time. The eerie apparition was produced by using a headshaped cutout on the set that was heavily backlit and filmed in smoke. "The time hole effect was an animated matte done directly on the aerial image camera," noted Houston. "We bipacked the sky background onto a series of animated mattes opening up into the time hole. As for the electric blue effect, Terry had wanted to create something interesting around the edges of the holes every time they opened up. This was then laid in as a separate pass on the same piece of equipment." Another technique was used for the twin time doors opening up in the subsequent Robin Hood segment. "We took portable five-foot-tall wooden frames on location with us to London's Epping Forest where we shot the Robin Hood stuff," said Gilliam. "Then we locked off the camera and had the guys either pass through the frames or at an angle beside them so that to the camera it would look as though they were passing through. The combined footage gave it all an odd appearance, as though the Bandits were being absorbed by "The twin holes were tough from an optical point of view," Houston noted, "because we had to run our animation and hardedged wipe right along the forest floor and beside some trees and it was very difficult to lose all that. So basically we just combined hard- and soft-edged mattes within the frames and took it directly out of frame. Terry had also shot some footage of blowing bits of colored paper which were supposed to be leaves. We laid that in - as well as some smoke - to pull your eye away from that hard- and soft-edged wipe." "The two segments with Napoleon and Robin Hood point out a basic theme of Time Bandits," noted Gilliam, "the notion of this little boy searching for his heroes and finding most of them coming up a little short. Napoleon is a drunken runt obsessed with height and Robin Hood is an upper-class twit who hasn't a clue about poor people. Even Agamemnon, who treats the lad well, turns him down when the boy wants to learn swordplay. Instead, Agamemnon teaches him magic tricks which he says at one point are far more useful in life. Kevin's having learned to deal realistically with hero worship is one of the reasons I left him alone at the end of the film without his parents. I felt he was now capable of looking after himself in life - not only because he had been through this adventure, but also because he had discovered that heroes are not usually what they're cracked up to be." Securing Sean Connery for the role of Agamemnon was something of a coup. "Originally we felt we had no chance of getting Sean. In fact, in the script, Michael and I had written a line that said, 'Agamemnon removes his helmet to reveal Sean Connery - or an actor of equal but cheaper stature. But providentially, Sean did get ahold of the script and agreed to be in the film. I think the fact that he would get to play a surrogate father appealed to him. Sean doesn't often get those kinds of roles." Both the Napoleon sequence and the Agamemnon segment are convincingly rendered in terms of historical detail. Benefiting from Gilliam's passion for period research and the truthful portrayal of past cultures, the look of the film also owed much to the work of production designer Milly Burns and costume creators James Acheson and Hazel Pethig. Locations included a Welch castle at Raglan used for the Napoleon sequence and the city of Ouarzazate in Morocco where the Agamemnon segment was filmed during a one-week period when Connery was available between other projects. By now, Kevin has accidentally become separated from his diminutive companions. Landing in ancient Greece, the youngster suddenly finds himself the unwitting savior of King Agamemnon who is battling a savage minotaur (Winston Dennis). Gilliam's design for this mythological creature incorporated a striking headpiece that resembled the skull of a bull. It was, in fact, a fiberglass prop actually cast from the remains of a real bull. 'We were careful to retain the original skin before we cast up the skull," Gilliam recalled. "We very gently peeled off all this rotting flesh and then reapplied it back onto the fiberglass head in great raggedy patches. If you are going to take a cast from something, I always say, cast it from life." Befriended by Agamemnon, Kevin is now treated to a lavish Grecian banquet. In a Fellini-like touch, an entire roasted cow is brought out to the assembled guests. Split open with a single sword stroke, the beast disgorges a cavity-full of fruit - plastic prop fruit actually. Cast up in polystyrene and covered with latex, the carcass was rigged with small explosive squibs, then manually triggered to split apart concurrent with the eviscerating sword. Kevin is eventually reunited with the Time Bandits on board the Titanic - a small but functional set built at Lee International. "The Titanic deck was laid down on big rockers," Gilliam recalled. "To suggest that the ship was sinking we could simply drop one end of the set and everything would slide downwards. I had the Bandits sitting around on little deck chairs which were

rigged on tracks and cables - I wanted a controlled slide for them. I didn't want to break those guys - they were irreplaceable." When the Titanic sinks, Kevin and his companions are tossed into the icy ocean - actually an exterior tank at Pinewood Studios one hundred feet in diameter. What follows is the ship itself slipping beneath the waves - a stock miniature shot produced originally in black-and-white for A Night to Remember and later colorized by effects master Wally Veevers for a subsequent Titanic project. Gilliam thought the shot was paced too slowly for Time Bandits, but resolved the matter handily by having it skip-framed to hasten the luxury liner's descent to its watery grave. With a platform hidden underwater for the actors to stand upon, whirlpool and wave machines to agitate the surface and large chunks of polystyrene to simulate icebergs, the Pinewood tank was convincingly transformed into the frigid North Atlantic. Kevin and the Bandits barely have time to lament their fate before they are plucked from the ocean by a mysterious force that deposits them in yet another alien sea. To accomplish the scene, footage of the actors falling into the tank was reverseprinted and then overlaid with an optical effect that resembled solarization. "At the time of Time Bandits," said Houston, "we had no processing facilities of our own and the labs said they could not help us. So that semi-solarized effect is just a combination of a partially exposed positive and some negative high-contrast stock. In some traveling matte work earlier in my career, I had observed that if you sandwiched those materials together, you would get what appears to be a solarized effect. So we used that." Floundering about in the alien sea, the Bandits are soon netted and brought aboard an unusual sailing vessel piloted by an ogre (Peter Vaughan) and his wife (Katherine Helmond). "One night at home I actually made a clay model of that ship," Gilliam reminisced, "just as a study guide. But then the most bizarre thing happened. The art department took the model literally. They pulled extremely precise plans off this thing and gave those to the construction crew saying, 'Build this exactly!' Well, I had never intended that. Weeks later, I came in and saw what trouble the construction guys were having and I said: 'Hey, forget it. Just fake it. Make it look like it's been assembled by a rather bad carpenter. ' Things went a lot smoother after that." Primarily constructed of plywood and fiberglass - twentyfive feet long and fifteen feet tall, with an obviously skewed center of gravity - the full-scale galleon was floated in the Pinewood tank and pulled along by underwater cabling. An interior set representing the ship's hold - where the ogre keeps the Bandits prisoner - was built at Lee International. Gilliam wanted the set to sway as though actually in the water. "Originally the set was built on a complicated system of hydraulic ramps. But they were so difficult and noisy in their operation that we undid them all and instead put a lot of old innertubes and tires and springs beneath the set. Then we just let the grips shake it about. A lot of the Time Bandits effects were done like this - manually and simply. Personally, I think films have tried to mechanize and computerize special effects too much. As a director, I have no patience for the ILM style of effects work. Sure, you can do some wonderful stuff with that approach - but when I'm shooting, I prefer just to get some good men offcamera doing their little tricks so I can direct everything right there on the set." The ogre makeup was accomplished by Gilliam's wife, Maggie Weston, an established makeup artist who would also contribute to Brazil and The Adventures of Baron Munchausen. The horns and tusks were cast in dental alginate while the nose, eye area and top of head were done as a single appliance. Finished with tufts of glued fur and careful blending, the ogre makeup took a daily average of between two and three hours to apply. Destined for the ogre's supper pot, the Bandits stage a comic mutiny and toss their captors overboard. Soon thereafter, a humongous giant appears from the depths and lifts their ship clear out of the water - revealing it to be his hatl "The giant was just one of those people with big earlobes who wander around the sea wearing ships on their head," Gilliam quipped. "When we first started casting for giants, we were looking at big guys - six-foot-seven and six-foot-nine - but they never photographed right. Suddenly I realized the problem was not height, but mass! So we got this wrestler named lan Muir who was pretty short - about five-foot-four - but almost as broad as he was tall. By sticking a very wide-angle lens down at his feet and shooting at about ninety-six frames per second, lan just became massive." The miniature ship-hat was fourteen inches long and molded from fiberglass to fit snugly over the wrestler's head. For the shot in which the giant abruptly lifts the ship from the sea, the camera was overcranked. As with all water effects, maintaining scale was a problem. In fact, Munchausen appears to have resigned himself to ending his days within the giant fish - a fate which is softened somewhat by the discovery that his two remaining servants, Gustavus and Adolphus, have also been swallowed and are engaged in a perpetual card game inside one of the wrecks. At the moment of petual card gamar inest Munchausen's darkest despair, Death appears at the card table. "None of the players seem to notice," said Conway, "but Death is dealing cards and flipping them across the table. Five people were operating the figure through a combination of puppeteering and animatronics. The puppet was controlled from behind - with one operator making its body turn, another making the head mechanisms work, a third making the wings twitch and so on. Sitting directly behind Death and covered in black velvet were two additional operators whose sole responsibility was to animate each arm and hand. There was a pistol grip arrangement jutting out just beyond each of the elbows. The two operators would manipulate these grips - and every movement of their fingers would translate correspondingly through a series of cables running into the puppet fingers." Sally again chases Death away. Moments later, the Baron's beloved Bucephalus magically appears by crashing through a rotting bulkhead. Reinvigorated, the Baron blows a handful of snuff out into the belly of the fish. The sea monster sneezes reflexively, propelling the Baron, his horse and his friends out through its blowhole. To accomplish the shot, a five-foot area around the monster's spout was crafted as a separate model and four-inch-tall beanbag puppets were ejected from it with a blast of compressed air and carbon dioxide. For a subsequent cut of a rowboat splashing down into the water, a quarter-scale fiberglass replica filled with concrete was elevated and released over the Pinewood tank. Safely reunited within the rowboat, Sally and the servants realize with despair that Munchausen is nowhere to be seen. Moments later, however, their leader surfaces beside the tiny craft. Grasping his own pigtail and giving a mighty pull, the Baron lifts himself and his horse clear out of the water! "We shot that in the Cinecitta pool," explained Conway. "First we had a stunt double sitting astride the top half of a full-scale dummy horse with a hydraulic rig pushing them up and turning the horse's neck. Then we cut to a wide shot of the Baron sitting astride a real horse floating in midair. We did that by wrapping a harness around the horse's midsection and concealing it with the saddle cloth. The animal's outer rib cage was duplicated in steel to prevent the harness from pressing into its flanks, and some very substantial nylon straps attached to that and ran underneath the belly and haunches of the horse. The stuntman just sat in the saddle, and we suspended them both above the water by a crane. We had to pump a lot of smoke into the scene to conceal the wires." Stunt coordinator Tony Smart - who orchestrated most of the segment - was also the company horse trainer. Stumbling ashore near the besieged city, the Baron finds his comrades are too old and lacking in confidence to take on the Turkish army by themselves. So the Baron forces the issue by giving himself over to the sultan, who promptly delivers his old nemesis to the chopping block for a public execution. What follows is an impressive pullback with the camera beginning in close on the Baron kneeling alone on the chopping block and then tracking back deep into the ranks of the Turkish army surrounding it. "That pullback was meant to suggest the Baron's isolation," Gilliam explained, "how he was totally alone and surrounded by all these troops. To do it we laid down about a hundred and fifty feet of track. Then we put the camera - an Arri BL3 - on a crane arm which extended out about ten feet in front of the dolly itself. That way when we tracked back there was a ten-foot gap between the dolly and the camera on the end of the crane, which gave us enough room for the extras to step around the dolly and back into the shot to cover up the tracks as we pulled through. The shot seems very fast, but it was not undercranked - it was all done in real time. The sense of speed is mainly the result of shooting with a 16mm lens. When you have people right next to a very wide-angle lens like that, they just rocket into frame." Unable to ignore the impending execution, the Baron's loyal

servants rally at the last possible moment to rescue their foolhardy leader. Supermarksman Adolphus fires a bullet that shatters the executioner's sword and Gustavus fills his lungs and literally blows away a squad of soldiers. As with scenes earlier in the film, the Gustavus breath effect was optically inserted at Peerless Camera. Shots of the soldiers being blown off their feet were accomplished with both live-action and miniature techniques. For closeups, ten live extras were rigged with wires on location and yanked backwards. Longer shots were done at Pinewood with eighteen one-foot-tall puppets being flung through the air by members of the crew. But the danger is not yet over. Berthold sees a Turk aiming his rifle at the Baron. In desperation, the speedster runs to warn his master just as the soldier fires. What follows is an outrageous race against time as Berthold tries to outrun the spinning bullet before the shot finds its mark. "The scenes of Berthold trying to outrace the bullet were done primarily with bluescreen," Conway said. "We used our pneumatically driven Berthold dummy for one shot - when it runs down the cliff, trips and falls over - but otherwise that sequence was done by filming Eric Idle and the bullet against the Cinecitta bluescreen at about four frames per second." Background plates for the sequence - tracking shots also filmed at about four frames per second - were photographed on the beach at Almeria by second unit director Michele Soavi. Berthold causes the bullet to ricochet back at the soldier who fired it, and the tide of battle now turns toward the Baron and his allies. In an inspired tactical maneuver, Gustavus blows a small mouse - actually a ball of fur transported via wind machine - to the feet of the sultan's war elephants. Shrieking in terror, the timid pachyderms stampede and retreat. "There were three elephants used in Baron Munchausen," recalled Conway. "All of them were fitted with little battle towers on their backs that were four feet high and three feet square and made of balsa wood. Inside the towers were lightweight cannons cast in fiberglass and equipped to fire off small charges. The charges were triggered electrically through a simple nailboard. I had worked with elephants before on Conan the Barbarian and I had learned that they are not to be trusted. One annoying thing elephants love to do is stand next to a person and whip him with their tails. During the battle scenes in Munchausen, we had to climb up on the elephants to reload the little fiberglass cannons every time they were fired. But the balsa towers were so lightweight that we had nothing to hold onto, so we were constantly falling off the elephants' backs. One day a friend who was working on the animal next to me fell off and plopped right into this big pile of elephant dung - and while he was sitting there in this mess the elephant came up and started whipping him with its tail. Talk about adding insult to injury! Elephants have an interesting sense of humor." With his other friends engaged, Albrecht now joins in the fray. Grasping a handful of anchor chains, the strongman reels in three wrecked ships from the harbor, swings the vessels over his head and flings them at the Turkish troops. "The ship effect was done sectionally," explained Conway. "We began with a shot of Winston Dennis pulling the chains out of the water. Those chains were tubular steel links that had been welded solid in a straight line. Each line ran down into the water and was attached to a sunken platform mounted on a track. Next there was a shot of the ships being pulled out of the water. Those were the same miniatures we had used inside the giant fish. We attached them to a tracked platform underwater and pulled them out with a tractor. The following shot had Albrecht standing on a rock swinging the chains around his head. Again those chains were rigid steel links. They were welded to a steel post that went down to a big hydraulic motor underneath the rock - sort of a merry-go-round arrangement. We attached Winston to a body harness on that rig. As his body turned, the chains turned also - and the rotating shaft was hidden by Winston's body and the false rock. All of this was filmed at the Cinecitta water tank. For the ships actually twirling in the air, we used small two-foot plastic models cobbled together in a fit of kit-bashing. We suspended them from wires attached to an overhead turntable. The chains here were very small - actually little watch chains that ran down out of the shot and connected to some metal arms below. During the shot, all we did was rotate the rig and let everything spin. The final shot of the boats crashing down used the large models again and a section of miniature beach with a painted background. We built the landscape at about a fifteen degree angle so we could drop the boats straight down and still have it look as though they were coming in at a slight angle." With hundreds of their comrades crushed by the falling ships, the demoralized Turks are finally routed. The Baron has saved the city! Munchausen and friends are given a triumphant parade into the town, but the vengeful enemy collaborator Horatio Jackson (Jonathan Pryce) - whose own political plans have been dashed by the Baron's victory - now takes his dreadful revenge. Hiding behind a large gargoyle in a bell tower, Jackson takes careful aim and shoots the Baron dead. The gargoyle then cracks open revealing a triumphant Death - a terrible specter which flies away from the incredulous marksman. "Death emerging from the gargoyle started on a set built in Rome," Conway said. "The first shot shows one of the gargoyle's wings breaking up next to Jonathan Pryce - that was a false plaster wing we had poured on location. I and one other person were actually behind it with a couple of hammers, whacking away at the thing until it fell apart. For a variety of reasons we could not do any more of that segment on location in Spain or at Cinecitta, so we took it back with us to Pinewood and shot the rest totally bluescreened. To get the gargoyle's head to crumble, it was actually blasted apart by a couple of guys with shotguns. That was a dicey situation because we also had to thrust the fullscale Death head up from behind the crumbling plaster head as it fell apart. Once the gargoyle has crumbled altogether, Death emerges in its full magnificence and flies away. To accomplish this shot, a quarter-scale rod puppet was affixed to a pylon and choreographed against a bluescreen by four operators - with most of the movements centering around the wings. Mortally wounded, the Baron lies dying in the street. A gravefaced physician dressed in black approaches and kneels over him. But the doctor is actually Death, who pulls - via a hidden wire - a bright throbbing light from the Baron's mouth. This visual representation of Munchausen's soul was actually an optical effect derived from a complex twisting sphere animated at Peerless by Tim Ollive. Interactive lighting was produced on set with a small strobe light wrapped in clear resin. To maximize its brightness, the strobe was electrically linked to the recording camera so that every time its shutter opened, the light would flash - producing an odd rippling effect. The city inhabitants honor their fallen savior with a royal funeral - but just as his body is being lowered into its grave, the scene abruptly switches back inside the Theatre Royal where a quite healthy Munchausen is finishing up the story he began at the start of the film. Denounced by Horatio Jackson as a charlatan, the Baron insists that the Turks have departed and leads a procession to the city gates to prove his assertion. In a stroke of fantasy turned reality, a wondering populace sees that the Turks have indeed withdrawn. Mounting Bucephalus and accompanied by his dog, the Baron says goodbye to all and then gallops away down a road lined with cheering crowds and a background cityscape. "Except for the Baron, his horse and a section of the crowd around him, that shot is essentially a matte painting," Houston revealed, "but we did add a few things. For example, we took a section of crowd from the right side of the Baron and moved it to his left side by flopping and repositioning the element. We also had a problem in that an overenthusiastic extra had taken off his hat and tossed it way up in the air during principal photography - with the result being that it sailed right across the matte line. So Doug Ferris had to continue that by animating a lookalike hat going up past the cutoff line and then falling back down. When the real hat fell back into frame, the animated one was wiped out of the shot." The final image in the film was also a matte shot. Bucephalus rears up among shafts of morning sunlight as the Baron waves and vanishes from sight. "What is wonderful and bizarre about the last shot," said Gilliam, "is that it is not the Baron and it is not his horse - it is not even his dog. It had always been our plan to shoot a really glorious shot for the finale - but there was no money at that point, so the scene was given over to Michele Soavi after the main unit cleared out of Almeria. He and his crew were the only ones left behind. It was a total grab shot. Michele found a white horse and managed to convince the owner - who was a woman - to dress up in the Baron's costume. I don't believe there was any makeup - maybe a fake beard. The dog was not even the right breed. All in all, it was pretty pathetic. But it was the best he could come up with, so he went ahead and took this shot of the Baron waving goodbye. Later, Dougie Ferris painted in a different hill and a different sky so that all that remained from the original shot was the false Baron, the false horse and the false dog." Some additional optical work was also required. "The live-action footage had been photographed quite large in the frame," Houston recalled, "and what we needed for the final shot in the movie was a wide shot. So first we had to optically reduce the Baron and Bucephalus by putting the separation masters on an optical printer at a greatly reduced position. That was then inserted into the matte painting as the live element. Finally, when the Baron disappears, he dissolves off with a very soft cut that was incorporated into all the separation masters." With his disappearance into legend, the adventures of Baron Munchausen come to an end - as does the film. For Terry Gilliam, the third entry in his trilogy signifies triumph over a dangerously prosaic world while at the same time offering an optimistic resolution to the uncertainty of Time Bandits and the pessimism of Brazil. Other resonances of content and form also abound. "Having completed my trilogy, I now notice certain odd similarities in all three films. One is the repetition of pullbacks. In Time Bandits, there is the cosmic zoom-out at the end. In Brazil, there is the long pullback at the end in the torture chamber. In Munchausen, there is the pullback from the chopping block. All I can say about this particular stylistic repetition is that my scripts usually have a shot marked 'PBTR' - pull back to reveal. Really, I think it's just a matter of stepping back from something. I also seem to have a persistent image of people being imprisoned in cages. Well, cages always seem to be with us, don't they? - and being trapped and imprisoned is one of my recurring nightmares. Frankly though, I don't much like analyzing my own work. Let the critics explore the motifs and hidden meanings. If pressed for an explanation, all I will say is that my trilogy culminates in a very personal victory - and that is the triumph of the imagination."
